The same framework transfers across five spiking classification and physics-informed neural network tasks. MNIST accuracy rises +13 pp; selected GNLSE errors drop up to 2500x and 325x. A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models

Ivan Moloshnikov ivan-rus@yandex.ru    Dmitry Kunitsyn Kunitsyn_DE@nrcki.ru    Alexander Sboev sag111@mail.ru    Maksim Skorokhodov Skorokhodov_MS@nrcki.ru    Roman Rybka Rybka_RB@nrcki.ru    Yuanchao Liu ycliuharbin@163.com organization=National Research Centre “Kurchatov Institute”, addressline=1 Akademika Kurchatova Square, city=Moscow, postcode=123182, state=Moscow, country=Russia organization=National Research Nuclear University MEPhI, addressline=31 Kashirskoye Shosse, city=Moscow, postcode=115409, state=Moscow, country=Russia organization=Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, addressline=9 Institutskiy Lane, city=Dolgoprudny, postcode=141701, state=Moscow, country=Russia organization=Harbin Institute of Technology, addressline=No. 92 West Dazhi Street, Nangang District, city=Harbin, postcode=150001, state=Heilongjiang, country=China
Abstract

Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles—analyst, coder, and recorder —with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks—spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) equations—the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have become the foundation of a new class of tools —agent systems that can not only respond to queries but also plan actions, use tools, execute code, and accumulate experience from previous steps Xi et al. (2023); Yao et al. (2023b). Such agents are already used in programming, ML engineering, and individual scientific disciplines Jimenez et al. (2024); Chan et al. (2024); Lu et al. (2024); Schmidgall et al. (2025); however, their use as a meta-optimizer for specialized neural network models remains understudied. A detailed review of related work is given in Section 2.

The quality of specialized neural network models depends strongly on the task: the representation of inputs and outputs, the method for decoding internal activity, the balance of loss-function terms, and other components must be selected anew for each problem, and no universal selection rule exists. In practice, this selection is performed manually, which makes the process labor-intensive and poorly reproducible. At the same time, models of different types can be decomposed into similar modules: input encoding and preprocessing, a trainable feature transformation, a decoding or output transformation, and a loss function. The tuning task is therefore reduced not to redesigning the entire network for every new problem but to modifying its individual modules, which enables a single tuning procedure applicable to models of different types.

Studies in which LLM agents are used as a general tool for automatic tuning of individual functional blocks of a model with a fixed architecture and training procedure are almost absent from the open literature (see Section 2). Existing systems focus either on programming tasks and the general ML cycle or on constructing a network from a textual task description. In contrast, the proposed framework does not build a network but modifies its predefined blocks using a single agent interaction pattern that does not depend on the particular application task.

The main contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We propose a multi-agent LLM framework for the automatic tuning of individual functional blocks of a neural network model (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    We show that the same framework transfers across five tasks with different types of information representation without changes to its internal structure (Section 5, Table 1).

  3. 3.

    We show that a detailed prompt improves the performance of less capable LLMs, bringing it closer to that of more advanced models (Section 5.2, Table 2).

  4. 4.

    The multi-agent framework improves the baseline models: on the spiking neural network (SNN) tasks (Tables 2 and 19), accuracy increases by 13% on MNIST and by 6% on the scikit-learn digits; on the physics-informed neural network (PINN) tasks (Section 5.4–5.6), the relative error decreases approximately 2500-fold for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) problem with a known analytical solution, and for problems without analytical solutions, the conservation error decreases approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE soliton–Gaussian run (more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations) and the mass drift decreases 14-fold for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) wave with a Gaussian perturbation.

2 Related Work

LLM agents can autonomously plan actions, use tools, and accumulate knowledge while solving multi-step tasks Xi et al. (2023). The ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) pattern has become a baseline architecture Yao et al. (2023b). Recent surveys Guo et al. (2024); Huang et al. (2024) identify typical components: a planning module (Chain-of-Thought Wei et al. (2022), Tree-of-Thoughts Yao et al. (2023a)), dynamic memory and self-reflection Shinn et al. (2023), calls to external tools, and multi-agent designs with role separation Chen et al. (2024). When agents act as meta-optimizers of neural network models, three of these components are essential: role separation distinguishes hypothesis formulation from its software implementation; logged memory prevents rejected variants from being proposed again; and a sandboxed execution environment is required to run generated code safely.

LLM agents have been applied to a diverse set of tasks. SWE-bench Jimenez et al. (2024) and MLE-Bench Chan et al. (2024) have become standard benchmarks for programming and automated ML: the medal rate of the first published o1-preview configuration with AIDE was 16.9 % Chan et al. (2024), while later agents increased this value to 64 % of medals on MLE-Bench Lite (MLE-STAR Nam et al. (2026), including 36 % gold medals) and to approximately 35 % across all difficulty levels (R&D-Agent on GPT-5) Yang et al. (2025). Similar multi-agent designs are used in materials discovery and biochemistry Takahara et al. (2025); Shi et al. (2026); Ghafarollahi and Buehler (2024); Swanson et al. (2025). Voyager Wang et al. (2023) demonstrates lifelong accumulation of a skill library in the form of executable code, which is close to the idea of logged hypotheses used in this work. Systems for automating the scientific cycle (The AI Scientist Lu et al. (2024); Yamada et al. (2025), Agent Laboratory Schmidgall et al. (2025)) and agent-based robot control Skorokhodov et al. (2025) have been developed in parallel; they show that autonomous research is possible in principle but do not incorporate domain-specific knowledge of PINNs or SNNs.

PINN quality depends on the choice of architecture, activations, the balance of loss-function terms, the distribution of collocation points, and the representation of inputs and outputs Moloshnikov et al. (2025b); separate heuristics have been proposed for each component, but no unified automatic procedure has been established. Lang-PINN He et al. (2025), the study closest to the agent-based approach, constructs a PINN from a textual task description but focuses on network construction rather than on selecting its functional blocks for a physical problem.

For SNNs, automatic approaches to selecting the architecture and its individual blocks rely on evolutionary algorithms and reinforcement learning Kim et al. (2022); Na et al. (2022); formally, neural architecture search (NAS) also includes the generation of individual functional modules within a predefined space of architectural variants. Unlike NAS, the proposed approach uses an LLM, exploits domain knowledge and knowledge of model properties, locally modifies a selected module of an existing network without searching a fixed space of variants, and stores the history of hypotheses in natural language, so that each subsequent iteration can use a substantive analysis of previous iterations rather than only their numerical results.

To the authors’ knowledge, the open literature contains no work in which LLM agents are used as a general tool for automatically tuning individual functional blocks of neural network models without redesigning the network itself. MLE-STAR Nam et al. (2026) is the closest agent system; the similarity is limited to two components: logged experiment memory and a sandboxed execution environment. MLE-STAR applies iterative code modifications with an update only when the metric improves on the outer loop, processes the entire ML script, selects the target block with a separate agent, assigns web search to a separate retriever agent, and involves more than ten agents.

3 Method: Multi-agent LLM framework

The framework optimizes a selected functional block while keeping the rest of the task pipeline fixed. Before a run, the Human Researcher specifies the task, the block that the agents may modify, the evaluation metric, the software contract for the generated code, and a baseline. These settings allow the same framework to be applied to different problems without changing its architecture or execution loop.

The framework is built on top of an OpenAI-compatible API and separates hypothesis generation, software implementation, and experiment documentation into three LLM roles. A sandboxed execution environment and an external experiment log close the iterative loop (Fig. 1). The framework consists of five main components:

  • •

    LLM Analyst receives the task prompt and the current experiment log. It proposes one hypothesis for the agent-modifiable block and expresses the idea as a technical specification with a fixed structure. If the Human Researcher provides a taxonomy of method classes, the Analyst also assigns the hypothesis to one of these classes.

  • •

    LLM Coder translates the technical specification into Python code. In addition to implementing the proposed method, the code must satisfy a task-specific software contract that defines the allowed dependencies, class names, call signatures, input and output shapes, and trainable parameters.

  • •

    Sandboxed execution environment (Docker) inserts the generated module into the fixed task pipeline, first performs a short functional test, and then evaluates a valid candidate. A runtime error is returned to the LLM Coder for correction, whereas the metric from a successful run is passed to the logging stage.

  • •

    LLM Recorder summarizes the specification, validated code, and evaluation result in a structured JSON record, including the method name, short description, and final hyperparameters.

  • •

    Experiment log is a table of structured records that serves as the external memory of the framework. Each record is assembled from the outputs of the pipeline stages and contains:

    • –

      a run identifier assigned by the framework;

    • –

      the experiment name and a short description generated by the LLM Recorder from the technical specification and validated code;

    • –

      the execution status assigned by the control loop from the functional-test and evaluation outcomes;

    • –

      the resulting target-metric value computed by the task-specific evaluation procedure for a successfully evaluated candidate;

    • –

      the method class selected by the LLM Analyst when a task-specific taxonomy is used;

    • –

      the final hyperparameter values extracted by the LLM Recorder from the validated generated code.

    Records with the With error status remain stored in the complete experiment log. Before the log is included in the Analyst prompt, the framework filters out these records, so the Analyst receives the baseline and successfully evaluated records only. The run budget counts only successfully evaluated records with the OK status.

The technical specification describes the method proposed by the Analyst, whereas the software contract defines the interface and constraints for the generated code. The agents may modify only the selected block; the rest of the task pipeline remains fixed. This separation allows generated code to be inserted and tested automatically. Applying the framework to a new task requires a new prompt, software contract, target metric, and baseline, but the agent roles and execution loop remain unchanged.

Baseline record.

Each framework run starts with a task-specific baseline record in the experiment log. This record evaluates the fixed pipeline with the simple baseline implementation of the modifiable block and provides the initial reference value of the target metric. The baseline implementations used in this study are defined in Section 4.

Standard and detailed Analyst prompts.

The framework supports two modes of hypothesis generation. The standard prompt contains the Analyst role, problem statement, target metric, implementation constraints, required format of the technical specification, and complete experiment log.

The detailed prompt retains these elements and adds a structured Chain-of-Thought procedure and a list of method classes specified by the Human Researcher for systematic exploration. Each hypothesis is assigned to one principal class, which is also stored in its experiment-log record, and the log is converted into a dynamically updated coverage map. For every class, the map reports the number of evaluated hypotheses, the best metric value, and a coverage status such as “not explored,” “limited data,” or “explored.” The map is included in the next Analyst prompt, which prioritizes suitable classes with little or no coverage and revisits an explored class only when a substantially different hypothesis is proposed. This mechanism structures an open natural-language search without reducing it to a finite list of implementations. The task-specific prompt configurations are described in Section 4; the detailed-mode prompt materials are provided in Supplementary Materials.

3.1 Run protocol

One framework run is a series with a task-specific number of successful iterations. At each iteration, one hypothesis is tested in six steps:

  1. 1.

    The Analyst receives the task prompt and the current experiment log. At the first iteration, the log contains only the baseline record. In detailed mode, the current coverage map is generated from the log and included in the prompt.

  2. 2.

    The Analyst creates a technical specification according to the prompt template. In detailed mode, the specification also identifies the method class.

  3. 3.

    The Coder implements the specification subject to the corresponding software contract.

  4. 4.

    The code undergoes an automatic functional test on a small sample in the sandboxed environment. If the test fails, the error message, generated code, and original specification are returned to the Coder. The Coder analyzes the reported error and rewrites the code while preserving the proposed method and software contract; the revised version is then tested again. If valid code cannot be obtained within 10 attempts, the experiment is assigned the With error status; it does not count toward the run budget, and the framework proceeds to a new hypothesis.

  5. 5.

    Code that passes the functional test is evaluated according to the task-specific evaluation protocol, and the resulting metric is assigned the OK status. The budgets, metrics, data-use rules, and repetition schemes used in this study are specified in Section 4.5 and the accompanying appendices.

  6. 6.

    The Recorder combines the specification, validated code, execution result, and fitted hyperparameters into a JSON record and appends it to the log. The updated log becomes the external memory for the next iteration.

4 Experimental setup

The same framework is applied to five tasks with different types of information representation: two spiking-network classification tasks, two boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and one boundary-value problem for the generalized Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.

4.1 SNN task: Correlation Classwise Network decoder

The classifier is based on a Correlation Classwise Network (CCN) spiking neural network Sboev et al. (2025); Kunitsyn et al. (2025), whose weights are trained using a local spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. Image pixels are normalized and encoded as correlated spike trains that serve as the network input. The output spike activity of the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons is then translated into a class label by the decoding module. The fixed part, which the framework cannot modify, comprises the input encoding, the CCN, and the recorded output activity vector 𝐫∈ℝK\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}; the agent-modifiable part is the Decoder⁡(𝐫)\mathrm{Decoder}(\mathbf{r}) module (Fig. 2). Its software contract permits fitting parameters from training activity and class labels but prohibits modifying the trained SNN, spike encoding, or recorded activity and prohibits error backpropagation. The decoder must return one valid class label per sample. We evaluate the method on two datasets: MNIST LeCun et al. (1998) (28×2828\times 28 images, N=784N=784 spike generators) and the scikit-learn digits dataset Pedregosa et al. (2011) (8×88\times 8, N=64N=64). Both contain 10 classes, so the network has K=10K=10 output LIF neurons. Accuracy is used as the target metric. As a baseline, we use an arg⁡max\arg\max decoder: the predicted class corresponds to the output neuron with the highest spike rate. Candidate selection uses only development data; the held-out test sets are unavailable to the agents, as detailed in Section B.1. Full details of the SNN model, the encoding scheme, the STDP rule, and the hyperparameters are given in Appendix B.

4.2 PINN tasks: GNLSE and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky

Two equations are investigated in this study. The first is the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation with the nonlinear correction (1) from Zavertyaev et al. (2024); Moloshnikov et al. (2025a), and the second is the generalized Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation (6) from Kudryashov (2026).

where the complex field q⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x,t)+i​v​(x,t)q(x,t)=u(x,t)+iv(x,t) is approximated by a fully connected network, while the equation (ℒp​d​e\mathcal{L}_{pde}), initial-condition (ℒi​c\mathcal{L}_{ic}), and boundary-condition (ℒb​c\mathcal{L}_{bc}) residuals enter the loss functional (ℒ\mathcal{L}) according to the Physics-Informed Neural Networks framework Raissi et al. (2019), a detailed description is given in the appendix A. In all configurations, β=0\beta=0.

The fixed part comprises the multilayer perceptron (MLP) architecture, loss functional, and training procedure. The agent-modifiable part comprises two transformations (Fig. 4): the input transformation FIF_{I}, which maps the coordinates (x,t)(x,t) to the MLP input features, and the output transformation FOF_{O}, which maps the MLP outputs and coordinates to the predicted physical field. For the GNLSE problems, the prediction consists of the two real components (u,v)(u,v); for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, it is the single real field uu. The agents may change the mathematical forms of FIF_{I} and FOF_{O} and may increase the intermediate MLP output dimension when required by FOF_{O}, but cannot modify the remaining architecture, loss functional, or training procedure. In the baseline, FIF_{I} passes (x,t)(x,t) to the MLP unchanged and FOF_{O} returns the raw MLP outputs. The framework is applied to two boundary-value problems for (1), which differ in the initial condition, domain, and target metric, and to one boundary-value problem for (6).

The second equation considered is a generalization of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation with nonlinear convection Kudryashov (2026). This generalization is important in high-temperature plasma research, where the nonlinear dependence of thermal conductivity must be taken into account Liu et al. (1976); Sudan and Rosenbluth (1976); Chen et al. (1977). We write the source equation for the scalar field v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) in the normalization

vt+vx​x+σ​vx​x​x+vx​x​x​x+γ​v​vx+χ​(v2)x​x=0.v_{t}+v_{xx}+\sigma v_{xxx}+v_{xxxx}+\gamma vv_{x}+\chi(v^{2})_{xx}=0. (5)

Here γ=2​β\gamma=2\beta is introduced to avoid confusion with the coefficient β\beta in (1). For β=3​σ\beta=3\sigma and σ=−1\sigma=-1, the coefficients used in this study are γ=2​β=6​σ=−6\gamma=2\beta=6\sigma=-6 and χ=3\chi=3. The corresponding exact traveling wave has the nonzero background −1/3-1/3. We therefore remove this background by introducing

v⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x,t)−13,v(x,t)=u(x,t)-\frac{1}{3},

so that the neural network approximates the zero-background scalar field u⁡(x,t)u(x,t). Under this change of variables, Eq. (5) becomes the differential equation in (6) (the complete substitution is given in Appendix A.2). Unlike (1), where the neural network approximates the complex field q⁡(x,t)q(x,t), this problem consequently has a single real-valued output, and the boundary conditions are zero for both the field and its second derivative. The general form of the loss functional follows the same three-term PINN scheme as for the GNLSE, but the MLP size, optimizer settings, and training budget differ; they are listed separately in Table 9. The agent-modifiable part comprises the same transformations FIF_{I} and FOF_{O} as in the GNLSE problems.

Traveling-wave problem with a Gaussian perturbation:

{ut−ux​x−ux​x​x+ux​x​x​x−6​u​ux+2​ux+3​(u2)x​x=0,u⁡(x,0)=12​cosh2⁡(x/2)+0.02​exp⁡[−(x+6)28],u(−30,t)=ux​x(−30,t)=0,u(40,t)=ux​x(40,t)=0,(x,t)∈[−30,40]×[0,10].\begin{cases}u_{t}-u_{xx}-u_{xxx}+u_{xxxx}-6uu_{x}+2u_{x}+3(u^{2})_{xx}=0,\\[2.0pt] u(x,0)=\dfrac{1}{2\cosh^{2}(x/2)}+0.02\,\exp\!\left[-\dfrac{(x+6)^{2}}{8}\right],\\[2.0pt] u(-30,t)=u_{xx}(-30,t)=0,\quad u(40,t)=u_{xx}(40,t)=0,\\[2.0pt] (x,t)\in[-30,40]\times[0,10].\end{cases} (6)

The unperturbed pulse has the form uex​(x,t)=12​cosh2⁡((x−t)/2)u_{\mathrm{ex}}(x,t)=\frac{1}{2\cosh^{2}((x-t)/2)} (speed 11, amplitude 1/21/2, starting at x0=0x_{0}=0); the Gaussian packet is located to the left (xg=−6x_{g}=-6, width w=2w=2) and catches up with the pulse at approximately t≈6t\approx 6, after which the perturbation intensifies. The complete analytical solution for this problem is unknown, so quality is assessed only by how well the network satisfies the boundary-value problem itself and by a physical diagnostic. The primary metric of the search is the mean absolute residual of the boundary-value problem,

Resbvp=14​(⟨|ℛKS|⟩+⟨|upred​(x,0)−u⁡(x,0)|⟩+⟨|upred|∂⟩+⟨|∂x​xupred|∂⟩),\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=\tfrac{1}{4}\Bigl(\langle|\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{KS}}|\rangle+\langle|u_{\mathrm{pred}}(x,0)-u(x,0)|\rangle+\langle|u_{\mathrm{pred}}|_{\partial}\rangle+\langle|\partial_{xx}u_{\mathrm{pred}}|_{\partial}\rangle\Bigr), (7)

where ℛKS\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{KS}} is the residual (22), the averages are taken over a uniform 1000×101000\times 10 grid in the domain, and ∂\partial denotes the two zero boundaries. The physical diagnostic is the relative mass drift of the predicted solution:

Δm(u)=maxk⁡|Mpred​(tk)−Mpred​(0)||Mpred​(0)|,Mpred​(t)=∫upred​(x,t)​𝑑x,\Delta_{m}^{(u)}=\max_{k}\frac{\bigl|M_{\mathrm{pred}}(t_{k})-M_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)\bigr|}{\bigl|M_{\mathrm{pred}}(0)\bigr|},\qquad M_{\mathrm{pred}}(t)=\int u_{\mathrm{pred}}(x,t)\,dx, (8)

with the maximum taken over ten uniformly spaced time slices tk∈[0,10]t_{k}\in[0,10].

4.3 Task-specific prompt configurations

The two universal Analyst modes defined in Section 3 are instantiated differently across the experiments. The PINN tasks use only the standard mode, with prompts that specify the differential equation, the modifiable transformations, the software contract, and the physical target metric; they do not use a method-family catalog, Chain-of-Thought procedure, or coverage map.

The SNN classification experiments compare the standard mode, denoted the simple prompt in the result tables, with the detailed mode. The simple prompt specifies the Analyst role, classification problem, target accuracy, data-use and implementation constraints, examples of admissible decoder types, required technical-specification format, and complete experiment log. The detailed prompt adds a researcher-defined taxonomy of 12 decoder-method classes, a structured Chain-of-Thought procedure for coverage and failure analysis, an explicit class field in the technical specification, and the dynamically updated coverage map. The 12 classes define broad areas of exploration rather than 12 fixed algorithms; each class may contain multiple feature transformations, decision rules, and hyperparameter settings, and hypotheses may combine methods from different classes. The complete class taxonomy and prompt texts are provided in Supplementary Section F.

4.4 Search baselines and budget: SNN decoder on MNIST

The quality reached by the framework depends both on the search performed by the LLM Analyst and on the constraints that the Human Researcher writes into the prompt. To separate these two contributions, we compare the framework with baselines that search the same space of decoders without an Analyst. All comparisons in this subsection are performed on MNIST, where the argmax baseline gives 79.88%79.88\,\%.

Shared search space.

The decoder catalog is a fixed discrete space of estimators with grids of their hyperparameters, together with the operators that build ensembles and multistage pipelines. It is specified once as a TPOT config_dict that is listed in Supplementary Section E.2 and its classes follow the decoder taxonomy of the detailed Analyst prompt (Section 4.3, Supplementary Materials). The Analyst prompt permits exactly the decoders contained in the catalog. The restriction reaches the systems in different ways: the agent receives it as text and can in principle depart from it, whereas the baselines receive it as a constraint on the sampler. We inspected the Experiment logs of all agent runs and found no record outside the catalog. The space of admissible decoders is therefore common to all systems, and they differ in the search strategy and in the selection protocol described below.

Compared configurations.

Three baseline configurations are compared with the framework, each with a budget of 250 evaluated decoders per run.

  • •

    Random Choice is an LLM-based sampler that draws decoder configurations from the same catalog through independent calls to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 deployed on a rented GPU, without a Chain-of-Thought stage and without a debugging cycle. Each call receives a compressed description of the catalog and returns one decoder configuration in JSON, sampled independently of the previous choices. The configuration is implemented and evaluated by the same sandboxed pipeline as an agent hypothesis. A call that yields a configuration outside the catalog, a configuration that fails the functional test, or a repetition of a configuration already recorded is discarded and does not enter the Experiment log. Calls are issued until the Experiment log contains 250 evaluated decoders.

  • •

    TPOT Olson et al. (2016) classic is the standard genetic algorithm with a population of 25 individuals and 9 generations, which together with the initial population gives 25×(9+1)=25025\times(9+1)=250 evaluated candidates.

  • •

    TPOT sequential uses a population of one individual and 249 consecutive generations, 1×(249+1)=2501\times(249+1)=250 candidates, so that the budget is preserved while population-level exploration is replaced by a single mutating lineage.

In both TPOT modes the search may combine models and build multistage processing sequences, because the corresponding operators are part of the catalog. TPOT samples and mutates pipelines according to its internal grammar, whereas Random Choice draws every configuration independently under an instruction to sample uniformly over the catalog.

Budget.

For the framework, the budget is the number of successfully evaluated records with the OK status. Records with the With error status remain stored in the complete Experiment log but do not count toward the budget and are excluded from the filtered log view passed to the Analyst. For Random Choice, the budget is the number of successfully evaluated decoder records; invalid calls discarded as described above do not count toward it. For TPOT, the budget is the number of fitted pipelines reported by the optimizer. In every configuration the budget is 250 per run, and every configuration was run 10 times. Within one run we take the best accuracy over the 250 evaluated decoders and the position at which it was first reached; Table 3 reports the smallest and the largest of these ten per-run values.

Selection and evaluation.

The baselines were run on the same trained SNN instances and the same output spike matrices as the prompt comparisons of Table 2, so every baseline run is matched with the corresponding agent run and the comparison is paired. The internal scoring rules of the compared systems are not identical. In the framework and in Random Choice, a candidate is scored on a validation set formed from the training set, and the value entered in the Experiment log (for the Analyst) is the mean over three random seeds. The held-out test set is not available to the Analyst (Section 4.5). TPOT selects its best pipeline by mean accuracy in five-fold cross-validation on the training set, after which the selected pipeline is retrained on the entire training set and evaluated once on the test set. The comparison in Table 3 is therefore made on the test accuracy of the best decoder of a run, which is defined in the same way for all systems.

4.5 Evaluation protocol

Run budget and thresholds.

The specified run budget (50 for the PINN tasks and 250 for the SNN tasks) counts only successful iterations; see Section 3.1 for the iteration steps. The target metric threshold (accuracy above 90 % for MNIST and 93 % for Digits; a decrease in Relh\mathrm{Rel}_{h} relative to the baseline for the single-soliton GNLSE problem, a decrease in Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} and Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} for the GNLSE problem with a Gaussian perturbation, and a decrease in Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem) provides a reference point for the analyst but is not a stopping criterion. Each hypothesis is evaluated with three random seeds in the single-soliton problem and with a single seed in the remaining two PINN problems, where one training run takes tens of minutes.

Compared configurations.

In both GNLSE problems, the baseline with identity FI,FOF_{I},F_{O} transformations is compared with three agent configurations: Perplexity Sonar (sonar-pro) Perplexity AI (2026), Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (qwen-qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct-2507) Qwen Team (2025), and Claude Opus 4.6 (anthropic-claude-opus-4.6); the Analyst prompt is the same for different LLMs. Because a complete agent run for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem is computationally expensive, we evaluated only Claude Opus 4.6, which produced the best results on the other tasks. The comparison for this problem is therefore limited to the Claude configuration and its baseline; different LLM models are not compared with one another. The Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 weights Qwen Team (2025) were downloaded from the model’s public repository. In the classification tasks, pairs ⟨\langlelanguage model, prompt⟩\rangle are compared: Claude Opus 4.6, Perplexity Sonar, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, each with the simple and detailed prompts defined in Section 4.3; the baseline is an argmax decoder based on the output spike rates of the LIF neurons. Ablation runs with the detailed prompt and the coverage-map section removed were also performed for all three models, while retaining the method catalog and Chain-of-Thought. Accuracy comparisons are provided in Tables 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18.

Metrics.

In the single-soliton problem, Relh\mathrm{Rel}_{h} is the final characteristic of a hypothesis; the best Relh\mathrm{Rel}_{h} (mean over three internal seeds) is reported. In the GNLSE problem with a Gaussian perturbation, hypotheses are ranked by the conservation error Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i}, while the boundary-value-problem residual Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} (4) is reported alongside it. The robustness of the best configurations was additionally tested using repeated runs (Appendix D). In the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, hypotheses are ranked by the boundary-value-problem residual Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} (7), and the mass drift Δm(u)\Delta_{m}^{(u)} (8) is reported as an independent physical diagnostic. In the classification tasks, the target metric is test accuracy, but during a run accuracy is evaluated on a validation set formed from the training set so that test-set accuracy is not entered in the experiment log.

Baseline model accuracies.

In the single-soliton problem, the identity-map baselines give Relh=4.69⋅10−2\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=4.69\cdot 10^{-2}, 5.51⋅10−25.51\cdot 10^{-2}, and 4.85⋅10−24.85\cdot 10^{-2} in the Sonar, Claude, and Qwen agent runs, respectively. In the GNLSE problem with a Gaussian perturbation, the corresponding single-run baselines give Reli=1.28⋅10−1\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=1.28\cdot 10^{-1}, 2.15⋅10−12.15\cdot 10^{-1}, and 1.85⋅10−11.85\cdot 10^{-1}; over n=10n=10 additional baseline trainings, mean is Reli=(1.65±0.18)⋅10−1\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=(1.65\pm 0.18)\cdot 10^{-1} (Table 11). In the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, the baseline gives Resbvp=1.41⋅10−3\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=1.41\cdot 10^{-3} and Δm(u)=9.31⋅10−2\Delta_{m}^{(u)}=9.31\cdot 10^{-2}. The SNN baseline (argmax over output spike rates, without Gaussian receptive fields (GRF) or bagging) gives an accuracy of 79.88 % on MNIST and 90.83 % on digits, consistent with previously published results Sboev et al. (2025). The gap between the datasets motivated target accuracies of 90 % on MNIST and 93 % on digits.

4.6 Statistical protocol

Repeated MNIST runs and statistical analysis.

To assess the effect of prompt structure, 10 complete runs, each comprising 250 iterations of agent search, were performed for every configuration. Two paired comparisons were performed for each of the three models: the simple prompt was compared with the full detailed prompt, and the detailed prompt with a coverage map was compared with its ablated version without the map. Each comparison comprised ten matched pairs of complete agent runs. Within each pair, the same trained SNN instance and identical output spike data were used, so differences between configurations were evaluated from paired differences in the maximum accuracy achieved.

For Perplexity Sonar, the difference between prompt variants was consistent across all ten runs: with the simple prompt, the maximum accuracy remained at the baseline level, whereas with the detailed prompt it exceeded 90 % in every case. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, the detailed prompt also increased the maxima relative to the baseline in all ten runs, although the magnitude of the improvement varied considerably. A paired statistical analysis over ten matched runs was performed for all three analyst models.

The prompt effect was tested using a two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test; two tests were performed for each of the three analyst models—“detailed versus simple” and “detailed versus detailed without the coverage map”—giving six tests to which the Holm correction for multiple comparisons was applied. Pairs were formed from runs with the same seed, which determines the framework initialization and the order of data presentation; in the Supplementary tables, the rows are ordered by decreasing accuracy of the detailed prompt rather than by seed number. For configurations in which the accuracy of the simple prompt exactly matched the baseline in every run, the paired test degenerates into a sign test, as reflected in the reported WW and pp values. The paired-analysis methodology and rationale for selecting the test are provided in Supplementary Section E. The unadjusted and Holm-adjusted pp values, together with the WW statistic for all six tests, are reported in Supplementary Section E; the difference is statistically significant in all six tests at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 after the Holm correction.

Repeated GNLSE trainings.

For the soliton with a Gaussian perturbation, the identity baseline and the two Claude configurations selected by Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} and Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} were each retrained ten times from independent random initializations. The random seeds were not recorded, so the three series are unpaired. The exported repeated-run data contain Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} and its two components but not Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}; consequently, this experiment characterizes robustness of invariant preservation only and does not establish a repeated-run success rate for the joint criterion.

5 Results

5.1 Summary across five tasks

The final results obtained by applying the same agent framework to five tasks are summarized in Table 1. Accuracy (higher is better) is used for the classification tasks, whereas a relative error or physical diagnostic (lower is better) is used for the PINN tasks. The improvement over the baseline is expressed in task-specific units: for classification tasks, the absolute accuracy increase Acc−Accbase\mathrm{Acc}-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{base}} is reported in percentage points, whereas for PINN tasks the error-reduction factor Errbase/Err\mathrm{Err}_{\mathrm{base}}/\mathrm{Err} is reported. The accuracy values and improvements shown in the table are rounded to integers. The corresponding unrounded accuracies are 79.88 and 92.83 % for MNIST (Table 2) and 90.83 and 96.67 % for digits (Table 19).

For the GNLSE soliton with a Gaussian perturbation, Table 1 reports the conservation error Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i}. For the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, it reports the mass drift Δm(u)\Delta_{m}^{(u)}, an independent physical diagnostic recorded alongside the optimized boundary-value-problem residual Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}; the latter decreases by a factor of 9.3 in the same run (Table 7). Each row compares a single best agent result with the corresponding identity baseline from the same analyst run.

For the GNLSE soliton with a Gaussian perturbation, robustness was additionally evaluated over ten independent trainings. These runs give Reli=(1.65±0.18)⋅10−1\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=(1.65\pm 0.18)\cdot 10^{-1} for the baseline, (1.42±0.59)⋅10−3(1.42\pm 0.59)\cdot 10^{-3} for the configuration selected by Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}, and (1.60±0.81)⋅10−3(1.60\pm 0.81)\cdot 10^{-3} for the configuration selected by Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i}. The corresponding reductions relative to the baseline mean are 116×116\times and 103×103\times, respectively (Table 11). Overall, the best agent configuration outperforms the baseline on the reported metric in all five tasks.

5.2 SNN classification results

The agent configurations on MNIST are compared in Table 2. For Claude Opus 4.6, the detailed prompt raises the mean maximum accuracy over ten runs paired by seed from 91.13±0.44%91.13\pm 0.44\,\% to 92.15±0.62%92.15\pm 0.62\,\%, and the best result from 91.65%91.65\,\% to 92.83%92.83\,\%. It gives the higher run maximum in eight of the ten pairs, and the two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test yields W=5W=5, p=0.0195p=0.0195, which remains significant after the Holm correction over the six tests of Section 4.6. The paired gain averages 1.02±0.901.02\pm 0.90 percentage points (Table 17), so for this model the effect is comparable to the spread between runs. For Perplexity Sonar and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, none of the 250 decoders proposed per run under the simple prompt outperformed the baseline, so the run maximum for both models matched the baseline of 79.88%79.88\,\% in all ten runs (std =0.00=0.00). The detailed prompt lifted both models above the baseline, though to different extents: for Perplexity Sonar, the individual-run maxima ranged from 90.93%90.93\,\% to 92.70%92.70\,\% with a mean of 91.76±0.56%91.76\pm 0.56\,\%, so the 90%90\,\% reference point was exceeded in all ten runs, whereas for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 the mean maximum was 85.88±2.42%85.88\pm 2.42\,\% and the best run reached 89.16%89.16\,\% without crossing it. For both models the prompt effect is significant by the same paired test (W=0W=0, p=0.00195p=0.00195, the minimum attainable value at n=10n=10; Tables 15 and 13).

On the scikit-learn digits dataset, the effect of the detailed prompt depended on the analyst model. For Claude Opus 4.6, the mean run maximum increased from 95.07±0.52%95.07\pm 0.52\,\% to 96.12±0.66%96.12\pm 0.66\,\%, with all ten runs reaching 93 %. For Perplexity Sonar, the mean changed from 93.44±0.57%93.44\pm 0.57\,\% to 93.31±0.93%93.31\pm 0.93\,\%, while the number of runs reaching 93 % decreased from 9/10 to 8/10, although the best observed result increased from 93.89 % to 94.17 %. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, the mean increased from 91.63±0.74%91.63\pm 0.74\,\% to 93.66±0.79%93.66\pm 0.79\,\%, and the number of runs reaching 93 % increased from 0/10 to 7/10.

5.3 Cost of the agent search

The positions kmink_{\min} and kmaxk_{\max} in Table 3 characterize the length of the search, not its computational cost. The framework and the Random Choice baseline are therefore compared by three quantities: the token usage per run, the cost of a complete run CrunC_{\mathrm{run}}, and the cost C∗C^{*} accumulated up to the earliest position kmink_{\min}. The token usage depends on the structure of the Analyst input, on the number of Coder attempts per iteration (Section 3.1), and on the size of the Recorder input.

Rates.

The Coder and the Recorder use gpt-5-mini in all configurations, at the provider’s public rate $0.25/$2.00 per M input/output tokens. For the Analyst, the rates in effect in June 2026 were $5/$25 per M input/output tokens for Claude Opus 4.6 and $1/$1 per M for Perplexity Sonar. Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 is deployed on a rented GPU and has no provider price, so its cost and the cost of Random Choice are given at the managed hosting rate for the same model class, $0.15/$0.60 per M tokens. Random Choice uses the same Qwen model in a single-agent configuration with 250 evaluated decoders without a Chain-of-Thought stage and without a debugging cycle. Its token usage was measured from the run logs in the same way as for the agent configurations.

Token usage.

The cost of a run is the sum of the token costs of the three roles of the framework, the Analyst, the Programmer, and the Recorder. For a role rr,

Cr=prin​Trin+prout​Trout,Crun=Can+Cpr+Crec,C_{r}=p_{r}^{\mathrm{in}}\,T_{r}^{\mathrm{in}}+p_{r}^{\mathrm{out}}\,T_{r}^{\mathrm{out}},\qquad C_{\mathrm{run}}=C_{\mathrm{an}}+C_{\mathrm{pr}}+C_{\mathrm{rec}}, (9)

where prp_{r} are the per-token rates and TrT_{r} are the token counts taken from the run logs.

The Analyst input at iteration ii consists of the fixed part of the detailed prompt (the role, problem statement, constraints, catalog of 12 method classes, coverage map, Chain-of-Thought instruction, and decoder examples), F=4085F=4085 tokens, and the experiment log of ii records of dlogd_{\log} tokens each. A log record is passed to the Analyst as a JSON object with the fields run_id, name, description, accuracy, and method_class, so its footprint dlogd_{\log} in the prompt exceeds the length dd of the description text itself, which is what the Recorder returns. Over the N=250N=250 accepted iterations of a run the Analyst also makes Nan−NN_{\mathrm{an}}-N additional calls that failed to produce an accepted decoder; at each such call the Analyst reads the log at its current length. Approximating the mean log length at the moment of a failed call by dlog​N/2d_{\log}N/2 — the average log length over the run — the total Analyst input is

Tanin=Nan​F+dlog​(N⁡(N+1)2+(Nan−N)​N2).T_{\mathrm{an}}^{\mathrm{in}}=N_{\mathrm{an}}F+d_{\log}\left(\frac{N(N+1)}{2}+(N_{\mathrm{an}}-N)\,\frac{N}{2}\right). (10)

The first term is the fixed prompt part paid at each of the NanN_{\mathrm{an}} Analyst calls; the second term collects the log tokens read during the NN accepted iterations (exact sum) and during the Nan−NN_{\mathrm{an}}-N failed calls (approximate).

The mean length of a log record in the Analyst prompt, measured with the cl100k_base tokenizer as the increment of the prompt length caused by one accepted record, is dlog=301d_{\log}=301 tokens for Claude Opus 4.6, 312 for Perplexity Sonar, and 317 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507; the description text alone accounts for 231, 244, and 252 of them. The numbers of Analyst calls per accepted iteration, measured on the same runs, gives Nan=265N_{\mathrm{an}}=265, 252, and 255 (Table 4). Equation (10) with these values gives Tanin=11.10T_{\mathrm{an}}^{\mathrm{in}}=11.10, 10.89, and 11.20 M input tokens per run, of which the fixed-prompt contribution Nan​FN_{\mathrm{an}}F is 1.08, 1.03, and 1.04 M and the log contribution is 10.02, 9.86, and 10.16 M. The Analyst output contains the Chain-of-Thought reasoning and the technical specification of the method. Its mean length per call, measured on the same runs, is 4399 tokens for Claude Opus 4.6, 2315 for Perplexity Sonar, and 2291 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, so that Tanout=Nan⋅Tan,callout=1.17T_{\mathrm{an}}^{\mathrm{out}}=N_{\mathrm{an}}\cdot T_{\mathrm{an,call}}^{\mathrm{out}}=1.17, 0.58, and 0.58 M per run.

The Coder receives its fixed prompt of 612 tokens together with the current specification and returns the Python implementation of the Decoding class; the mean length of accepted code is 4982 tokens for Claude Opus 4.6, 3749 for Perplexity Sonar, and 2513 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. If the code does not pass the functional test, the failing code and its trace stay in the dialogue and are re-read at every subsequent attempt of the same iteration, so the Coder input grows quadratically with the length of the debugging chain. The debug rate, measured from the runs, is 3.31 Coder calls per accepted iteration for Claude Opus 4.6, 1.70 for Perplexity Sonar, and 2.05 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, with mean failed-attempt lengths of 5991, 4641, and 2724 tokens, respectively. Reconstructing every Coder dialogue of the runs token by token gives Coder token counts per run of 12.98, 2.40, and 2.79 M for the input and 4.66, 1.73, and 1.32 M for the output.

The Recorder receives its own prompt of 99 tokens together with the Coder prompt and the accepted code, and returns the description of length dd, so that Trecin=2.61T_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{in}}=2.61, 1.71, and 1.38 M and Trecout=N​d=0.058T_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{out}}=Nd=0.058, 0.061, and 0.063 M per run. Summation of (9) over the three roles gives complete-run costs of $97.99, $16.08, and $5.85 for Claude Opus 4.6, Perplexity Sonar, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, with the Analyst contributing $84.66, $11.47, and $2.03, and costs up to kmink_{\min} of $0.37, $0.21, and $0.26.

Cost of Random Choice.

Random Choice gives the lowest token usage among the compared systems. Each mini-call contains the catalog of method classes as input and one JSON decoder configuration as output; at about 800 input and 120 output tokens per call and 347 calls per run, the run requires 0.28 M input and 0.042 M output tokens. These values are 40 and 14 times smaller than the Analyst token counts of the Qwen agent with the detailed prompt (11.20 M and 0.58 M). In accuracy the two configurations are close: the per-run maxima of Random Choice lie between 89.48 and 89.93 %, those of the Qwen agent between 82.28 and 89.16 % (Table 3), and neither configuration reaches the 90 % threshold. When Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 is used free of charge, Crun=0C_{\mathrm{run}}=0 for both configurations, and they differ only in token usage and in C∗C^{*}. At the managed rate for this model class, the Analyst cost differs by a factor of 29 ($0.07 for Random Choice against $2.03 for the agent framework with Qwen as the LLM Analyst), and with the Coder and the Recorder included by a factor of 84 ($0.07 against $5.85, Table 4). Sampling of the same catalog using Random Choice method is therefore two orders of magnitude cheaper than the Qwen agent framework at comparable accuracy. Both proprietary Analysts with the detailed prompt exceed it: their minimum run maxima are 90.93 % for Perplexity Sonar and 91.22 % for Claude Opus 4.6, against 89.93 % for Random Choice. The framework is thus preferable to sampling of the same catalog when the Analyst model is sufficiently strong; for a weak Analyst, the additional cost and the additional components of the framework are not compensated by the accuracy.

5.4 PINN results: single soliton

The first PINN problem (GNLSE, α=0.1\alpha=0.1, β=0\beta=0) has an analytical solution and therefore provides a transparent test of the framework: the agent can embed the explicit form of the one-soliton solution in the FI,FOF_{I},F_{O} blocks, and the resulting metrics reflect the correctness of such a “hinted” representation rather than an independent search for a nontrivial technique. The results are summarized in Table 5. Because each agent run includes its own three-seed identity baseline, each reduction factor is calculated against the baseline from the same run. The best Claude Opus 4.6 hypothesis gives Relh=2.21⋅10−5\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=2.21\cdot 10^{-5}, a 24912491-fold reduction from 5.51⋅10−25.51\cdot 10^{-2}. The best sonar-pro hypothesis reduces Relh\mathrm{Rel}_{h} from 4.69⋅10−24.69\cdot 10^{-2} to 1.97⋅10−41.97\cdot 10^{-4} (238×238\times), while Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 reduces it from 4.85⋅10−24.85\cdot 10^{-2} to 8.86⋅10−38.86\cdot 10^{-3} (5.48×5.48\times). Because the problem permits substitution of the analytical formula, these figures should not be interpreted as a measure of a complex search; the substantive test is deferred to the second problem.

The best sonar-pro configuration is tw_nonlinear_pinn_core. Its FIF_{I} supplies a normalized traveling-wave coordinate, normalized time, and a local nonlinearity-density feature; FOF_{O} uses the analytical traveling-wave amplitude and phase and interprets the MLP outputs as bounded amplitude and phase corrections. The best Claude Opus 4.6 configuration, PCDS-LCC-EXP-NLOG-MIXCROSS, uses seven analytical features, including normalized and logarithmic envelopes and two amplitude–time cross-features, while FOF_{O} applies time-gated exponential amplitude and additive phase corrections with separate envelope weights. The best Qwen configuration, LogPhaseHybridNorm, normalizes the analytical soliton coordinate at the input and reconstructs the field from the analytical amplitude and carrier phase multiplied by learned complex corrections. Thus, all three best configurations exploit the known soliton structure in both the representation and the reconstruction. A detailed analysis of the hypotheses is provided in Appendix C.

5.5 PINN results: soliton with gaussian perturbation

The second PINN problem (GNLSE, α=0.3\alpha=0.3, β=0\beta=0; the initial condition is a soliton with a superimposed Gaussian perturbation) has no analytical solution, so the agent cannot embed a ready-made formula and must search for a substantive representation. The search is driven by Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} (4) and Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i}; the reruns reported here do not include Relh\mathrm{Rel}_{h}. The human-designed PINN from prior work has Resbvp=9.11⋅10−5\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=9.11\cdot 10^{-5} and Reli=9.87⋅10−4\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=9.87\cdot 10^{-4}. The single-run results are summarized in Table 6. The shared identity baseline combines the lowest Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} and the lowest Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} observed across the analyst runs, and each reduction factor is computed relative to its Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i}. The 325×325\times improvement is obtained relative to the identity baseline from the same Claude Opus 4.6 run, whereas the 194×194\times improvement is obtained relative to the shared cross-run reference baseline. The best Claude Opus 4.6 configuration by conservation error, SPM_XPM_CorrWidth_SplitScale_HighP, reduces Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} from 1.28⋅10−11.28\cdot 10^{-1} to 6.61⋅10−46.61\cdot 10^{-4} (194×194\times) while giving Resbvp=3.95⋅10−5\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=3.95\cdot 10^{-5}. A different Claude configuration, SplitAlpha_ExpPhase_HighP, gives the lowest residual, Resbvp=2.08⋅10−5\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=2.08\cdot 10^{-5}, with Reli=1.40⋅10−3\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=1.40\cdot 10^{-3}. The best sonar-pro hypothesis by Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} improves this metric 20×20\times, but its Resbvp=2.37⋅10−2\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=2.37\cdot 10^{-2} is worse than the shared baseline; the best Qwen hypothesis improves Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} only 1.36×1.36\times and likewise does not improve the baseline residual. Thus, only the Claude hypotheses improve both reported criteria substantially.

Ten additional trainings from random initializations were performed for the identity baseline and for both Claude configurations. The configuration selected by Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} gives Reli=(1.42±0.59)⋅10−3\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=(1.42\pm 0.59)\cdot 10^{-3}, a 116×116\times reduction from the repeated baseline mean, while the configuration selected by Reli\mathrm{Rel}_{i} gives (1.60±0.81)⋅10−3(1.60\pm 0.81)\cdot 10^{-3}, a 103×103\times reduction. The repeated-run export does not contain Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}, so these series confirm robustness of the invariant error but not of the joint criterion. Details are provided in Appendix D.

5.6 PINN results: Kuramoto–Sivashinsky

In the traveling-wave problem with a Gaussian perturbation, the Claude Opus 4.6 agent generated the FI,FOF_{I},F_{O} transformations while minimizing the boundary-value-problem residual Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}. The mass drift Δm(u)\Delta_{m}^{(u)} was recorded alongside it but did not drive the search. The best values are summarized in Table 7, and the two metrics are computed by different hypotheses.

On the primary metric (Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}), the best architecture is MultiplicativeIC_DualAdditive_DualZoom, which reduces Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} from the baseline value of 1.41⋅10−31.41\cdot 10^{-3} to 1.511⋅10−41.511\cdot 10^{-4}, a factor of 9.3. On the physical diagnostic, the best architecture is BoundedMultAdd_SechZoom_DualPhase, which reduces Δm(u)\Delta_{m}^{(u)} from 9.31⋅10−29.31\cdot 10^{-2} to 6.56⋅10−36.56\cdot 10^{-3}, an approximately 1414-fold reduction, while also improving Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} by a factor of 8.3.

Both winning hypotheses share a multiplicative–additive decomposition u^=u⁡(x,0)​e−α​t​(1+t​γm​N1)+t​W​(x)​(γ1​N2+γ2​N3)\hat{u}=u(x,0)\,e^{-\alpha t}\bigl(1+t\,\gamma_{m}N_{1}\bigr)+t\,W(x)\bigl(\gamma_{1}N_{2}+\gamma_{2}N_{3}\bigr), in which N1,2,3N_{1,2,3} are the three MLP outputs, the initial profile is embedded exactly at t=0t=0, the window W⁡(x)=sL​sRW(x)=s_{L}s_{R} built from the two normalized distances to the boundaries vanishes at x=−30x=-30 and x=40x=40, and the input block supplies features in the co-moving coordinate ξ=x−t\xi=x-t — a rescaled tanh⁡(ξ/λ)\tanh(\xi/\lambda), the profile sech2​(ξ/2)\mathrm{sech}^{2}(\xi/2) of the unperturbed pulse, and a phase marker sin⁡(π​t/6)\sin(\pi t/6) of the collision. The hypothesis that wins on mass drift differs in one detail: the multiplicative channel is bounded, N1↦tanh⁡(N1)N_{1}\mapsto\tanh(N_{1}), so the correction cannot rescale the embedded initial profile without limit. This bound costs little in terms of the residual but keeps the integral quantity M=∫u​𝑑xM=\int u\,dx an order of magnitude closer to its initial value, which illustrates that the two criteria are not interchangeable.

6 Ablation studies

6.1 Simple and detailed prompts

This ablation compares the simple and detailed SNN prompt configurations defined in Section 4.3. The detailed configuration combines the method-class taxonomy, structured Chain-of-Thought, and coverage map described by the general framework in Section 3. The full Analyst and Coder prompts are provided in Supplementary Section F.

The MNIST configurations are compared in Table 2. For Claude Opus 4.6, the detailed prompt increased the mean maximum accuracy over ten matched complete runs from 91.13±0.44%91.13\pm 0.44\,\% to 92.15±0.62%92.15\pm 0.62\,\%, and the best result from 91.65 % to 92.83 %. The difference between the prompt variants is confirmed by a two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test (W=5W=5, p=0.0195p=0.0195), with the detailed prompt yielding higher accuracy in eight of ten pairs; the mean paired difference is 1.02±0.901.02\pm 0.90 percentage points (Table 17), meaning that the effect is comparable in magnitude to the between-run variation.

Ten complete runs were performed with each prompt variant for Perplexity Sonar and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. With the simple prompt, none of the 250 decoders proposed per run outperformed the baseline, so the run maximum for both models exactly matched the baseline of 79.88 % in all ten cases. The detailed prompt changed the results of both models, but to different extents. The 90 % threshold was fixed before the run series as a reference point for MNIST; for the digits dataset, where the baseline is already 90.83 %, an analogous reference point was set at 93 % Section 4.5 and is not used in the tables in this section. For Perplexity Sonar, the individual-run maxima ranged from 90.93 % to 92.70 % (Table 15), with a mean of 91.76±0.56%91.76\pm 0.56\,\%, so the 90 % threshold was exceeded in all ten runs. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, the mean maximum was 85.88±2.42%85.88\pm 2.42\,\%, and the best run reached 89.16 % without exceeding the specified 90 % threshold. The difference between the prompt variants for both models is confirmed by a two-sided exact paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

A run-by-run comparison between the simple and detailed prompts for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 is provided in Table 13. With the simple prompt, accuracy remained at the baseline level of 79.88%79.88\,\% in all ten runs. The detailed prompt provided gains ranging from 2.402.40 to 9.289.28 percentage points in individual runs. The mean maximum accuracy was 85.88±2.42%85.88\pm 2.42\,\%, and the best result was 89.16%89.16\,\%. The high variability (std=2.42\mathrm{std}=2.42 percentage points at n=10n=10) indicates instability of the search when this model is used.

6.2 Coverage-map ablation

The ablation experiment excluding the coverage map was performed for all three analyst models (Tables 14, 16, and 18). For Claude Opus 4.6, removing the map reduces the mean maximum to 91.02±0.25%91.02\pm 0.25\,\%, which is 1.141.14 percentage points below the detailed prompt (92.15%92.15\,\%) and nearly matches the level of the simple prompt (91.13%91.13\,\%). All ten runs nevertheless retain accuracy above 90 %, indicating that the coverage map has little effect on the result for the strong model. For Perplexity Sonar, removing the map reduces the mean maximum to 82.34±0.70%82.34\pm 0.70\,\% (Δ=9.42\Delta=9.42 percentage points), and no run reaches the threshold. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, the mean maximum falls to 80.18±0.45%80.18\pm 0.45\,\% (Δ=5.70\Delta=5.70 percentage points), effectively returning to the baseline level of 79.88 %: the coverage map proves to be the key component that enabled this model to improve over the baseline argmax decoder (the class label is assigned by the neuron with the highest spike rate).

7 Discussion

The experiments show that prompt detail can partially compensate for the limitations of the analyst model, although the degree of compensation depends on the LLM used. Claude Opus 4.6 achieves accuracy above 90 % with both prompt variants. With the simple prompt, Perplexity Sonar remains at the baseline level in all ten complete runs, but with the detailed prompt it consistently exceeds 90 % and reaches the level of Claude Opus 4.6. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, the detailed prompt also produces a substantial gain: the best result increases from 79.88 % to 89.16 %. At the same time, the higher variability of the maxima (85.88±2.42%85.88\pm 2.42\,\%) and the absence of any run with a maximum accuracy above 90 % show that the instruction structure does not fully compensate for the limitations of this model. When search cost is taken into account (Table 4), the advantage of Claude Opus 4.6 also persists in economic terms: despite the highest cost per run ($98 versus $16 for Sonar), it reaches its best decoder after only kmin=2k_{\min}=2 to kmax=43k_{\max}=43 evaluated candidates (Table 3), which makes the cost of reaching the best result comparable to that of Sonar ($0.37 versus $0.21), whereas Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, deployed on a rented GPU, costs less than both proprietary models ($5.90 per run at the managed rate for the same model class, with the Analyst alone contributing $2.00) but still fails to reach the target threshold over the full run.

In every task, the agent finds a technique tied to the physics of the problem: class-conditional spike-rate statistics for the CCN, the soliton structure of the solution for the Schrödinger equation, and a phase-separated representation of the pulse–perturbation interaction for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation. The second PINN problem (a soliton with a Gaussian perturbation) is particularly informative: its analytical solution is unknown, so the gain cannot be reduced to substituting a ready-made formula, and the best configuration (Claude Opus 4.6) improves the conservation of the integrals of motion by more than an order of magnitude. In the KS problem, the improvement appears in a different physical diagnostic, namely mass drift. All five experiments are nevertheless handled by the same framework without changes to its internal structure.

8 Limitations

Despite the results reported above, the present study has several limitations that should be taken into account when interpreting the findings and when comparing our system with alternative approaches.

  • •

    Restricted search space. The agent modifies a fixed catalogue of editable blocks (encoders, neuron models, connectivity schemes for SNNs; loss weights, activation functions and sampling strategies for PINNs). Structural transformations that fall outside this catalogue – for example, adding auxiliary networks or replacing the entire training paradigm – cannot be discovered by the current agent and would require an extended action space.

  • •

    Flat experiment log without a hypothesis graph. The Recorder stores runs as a chronological JSON log; it does not maintain a directed acyclic graph of hypotheses and their dependencies. As a consequence, the Analyst re-derives relations between experiments from the log at every step, which limits the depth of multi-step reasoning that can be sustained over long sessions.

  • •

    Bounded number of iterations. All reported runs are capped at 250250 iterations for SNN tasks and 5050 iterations for PINN tasks. These bounds were chosen to keep the wall-clock cost reproducible within the budgets reported in Table 4, but they also mean that the accuracy and relative-error values in Sections 5.2, 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6 are lower bounds on what the agent can eventually reach with a larger budget.

  • •

    Single-seed evaluation in part of the regimes. For the most expensive configurations (Claude Opus 4.6 on the generalised nonlinear Schrödinger equation and on the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky benchmark) we report a single seed per configuration; the ten-run averages for best models are given only for the soliton with a Gaussian perturbation case. A full multi-seed sweep for every LLM/task pair is left for future work.

  • •

    Dependence on proprietary LLM APIs. Two of the three evaluated models (Claude Opus 4.6 and Perplexity Sonar) are accessed through commercial APIs; their availability, pricing and behaviour may change between the time of the experiments and the time of reproduction. The open-weights Qwen3-30B-A3B run is provided as a partial mitigation, but its cost/quality trade-off is not directly comparable to the proprietary systems.

  • •

    No head-to-head comparison with LLM-based NAS baselines. The reported baselines are a random-choice controller and the state-of-the-art results reported in the cited references. A direct comparison with recent LLM-driven neural-architecture-search systems on the same tasks and under the same iteration and cost budgets is desirable but was outside the scope of the present paper; we consider it the natural next step of this line of research.

9 Conclusion

To date, automatic tuning of neural networks has been carried out mainly within the framework of an allocated single metric of the given competition: agent-based systems optimize the entire ML script, NAS approaches search over architectures according to accuracy, and PINN frameworks train networks to minimize the relative error. For tasks whose quality is defined by a multidimensional signal—by the conservation of a set of physical invariants or by additional structural requirements—frameworks of a different class are required. The results reported in this paper demonstrate the robustness and generalization ability of the proposed multi-agent framework, which consists of an analyst, a programmer, and a recorder, together with a sandboxed execution environment and an experiment log serving as external memory, on tasks of different nature without changes to its internal structure.

The same unchanged framework was applied to five tasks with different types of information representation: accuracy increased from 79.88 % to 92.83 % on MNIST and from 90.83 % to 96.67 % on digits; in the single-soliton PINN problem, the relative amplitude error decreased by a factor of approximately 2491; in the more complex problem with a Gaussian perturbation and no known analytical solution, the conservation error of the integrals of motion decreased by a factor of approximately 325 in the selected run and by factors of 116 and 103, respectively, based on the mean errors over ten additional trainings of the residual-selected and invariant-selected configurations (Table 11); and in the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, the boundary-value-problem residual decreased by a factor of 9.3 and mass drift by a factor of 14 (Tables 1 and 7). A separate result concerns the interaction between the analyst model and prompt structure. On MNIST, the detailed prompt enabled Perplexity Sonar to exceed 90 % accuracy in all ten complete runs and to reach a maximum of 92.70 %, close to the result of Claude Opus 4.6. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, maximum accuracy increased from the baseline level of 79.88 % to 89.16 %, but the target threshold was not reached. Prompt design can therefore substantially improve the performance of a less capable LLM, but only partially compensates for differences between models.

Future work includes increasing the complexity of the PINN problem (the interaction of two solitons and other regimes without analytical solutions), jointly tuning several blocks (the decoder and plasticity rules for the SNN), and constructing models that account for the constraints of neuromorphic systems.

Appendix A Baseline PINN model

The model problem is a boundary-value problem for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) with cubic–quintic nonlinearity:

{i​qt+qx​x+|q|2​q​(1−α​|q|2+β​|q|4)=0,q​(x, 0)=q~​(x, 0),q(xmin,t)=0,q(xmax,t)=0,(x,t)∈[xmin,xmax]×[tmin,tmax].\begin{cases}i\,q_{t}+q_{xx}+|q|^{2}q\,\bigl(1-\alpha|q|^{2}+\beta|q|^{4}\bigr)=0,\\[4.0pt] q(x,\,0)=\tilde{q}(x,\,0),\\[2.0pt] q(x_{\min},\,t)=0,\quad q(x_{\max},\,t)=0,\\[2.0pt] (x,t)\in[x_{\min},x_{\max}]\times[t_{\min},t_{\max}].\end{cases} (11)

In all configurations, β=0\beta=0; the quintic term is retained in the equation for generality. Two configurations are considered. In the single-soliton problem, α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and the domain is (x,t)∈[−25,25]×[0,3](x,t)\in[-25,25]\times[0,3]; the initial profile is specified by the analytical soliton solution:

q~​(x,0)=μ​z(12​z+1)2−α​μ3​z2⋅ei⁡(k​x+θ0),z=eμ​(x−x0),\tilde{q}(x,0)=\sqrt{\frac{\mu z}{\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}z+1\bigr)^{2}-\tfrac{\alpha\mu}{3}z^{2}}}\cdot e^{i(kx+\theta_{0})},\qquad z=e^{\sqrt{\mu}(x-x_{0})}, (12)

where k=1k=1, w=0.88w=0.88, x0=0x_{0}=0, θ0=0\theta_{0}=0 and μ=4​(k2−w)\mu=4(k^{2}-w). The complex field is decomposed into two real components: q⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x,t)+i​v​(x,t)q(x,t)=u(x,t)+i\,v(x,t). The analytical soliton is used as the reference when calculating the error.

In the second configuration (a soliton with a Gaussian perturbation), α=0.3\alpha=0.3, the domain is extended to (x,t)∈[−50,50]×[0,25](x,t)\in[-50,50]\times[0,25], and the initial condition is the sum of the soliton profile (12) (with x0=−30x_{0}=-30) and a real-valued Gaussian packet:

q(x,0)=q2(x,0)+0.2e−x2/50,q(x,0)=q_{2}(x,0)+0.2\,e^{-x^{2}/50}, (13)

where q2q_{2} coincides with (12) for the specified parameters, equivalently Agexp[−(x−Bg)2/(2Cg2)]A_{g}\exp[-(x-B_{g})^{2}/(2C_{g}^{2})] with Ag=0.2A_{g}=0.2, Bg=0B_{g}=0, and Cg=5C_{g}=5 (the printed Cg2C_{g}^{2} in Zavertyaev et al. (2024) is a typographical error, must be 2​Cg22C_{g}^{2}). The analytical solution is unknown. A PINN field from Zavertyaev et al. (2024) is retained as an auxiliary amplitude reference. On [−50,50]×[0,25][-50,50]\times[0,25] that field has Resbvp=9.11⋅10−5\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}}=9.11\cdot 10^{-5} and Reli=9.87⋅10−4\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=9.87\cdot 10^{-4}. The baseline network in this configuration is deeper, with 4 hidden layers of 64 neurons each, and collocation-point sampling is adaptive (version v3 from Moloshnikov et al. (2025b), regenerated every 1000 iterations with coefficient λ2=0.01\lambda_{2}=0.01 in Pr​lP_{r}l in Eq. 6 of Moloshnikov et al. (2025b)).

The primary metrics of the search are Resbvp\mathrm{Res}_{\mathrm{bvp}} (4) and the relative conservation error of the integrals of motion Reli=Reli1+Reli2\mathrm{Rel}_{i}=\mathrm{Rel}_{i_{1}}+\mathrm{Rel}_{i_{2}}; Relh\mathrm{Rel}_{h} has lowest priority.

The baseline is a fully connected network MLP:ℝ2→ℝ2\mathrm{MLP}\colon\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}, (x,t)↦(u,v)(x,t)\mapsto(u,v), with two hidden layers of 32 neurons each and sin\sin activation. In the modified architecture, two tunable blocks, FI​(x,t)F_{I}(x,t) and FO​(u,v,x,t)F_{O}(u,v,x,t), are attached to the MLP; both blocks are identity mappings in the baseline. The complete set of hyperparameters for both configurations is summarized in Table 8. The loss functional consists of three terms with equal weights:

ℒ=ℒpde+ℒic+ℒbc,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pde}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ic}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bc}}, (14)

where ℒpde\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pde}} is the mean squared residual of Eq. (11) at the collocation points, ℒic\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ic}} is the initial-condition error, and ℒbc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bc}} is the boundary-condition error. The derivatives qt,qx​xq_{t},q_{xx} are obtained by TensorFlow automatic differentiation. For the single-soliton problem the metric is:

Relh=‖htrue−hpred‖2‖htrue‖2,h=u2+v2.\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=\frac{\|h_{\mathrm{true}}-h_{\mathrm{pred}}\|_{2}}{\|h_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{2}},\qquad h=\sqrt{u^{2}+v^{2}}. (15)

A.1 Kuramoto–Sivashinsky baseline hyperparameters

The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem uses its own baseline configuration, summarized in Table 9. It differs from the GNLSE configurations in three respects. First, the network output is a single real scalar. Second, the fourth derivative in the residual makes the raw loss stiff, so the residual is divided by R0=10R_{0}=10 before squaring, the learning rate is lowered to 5⋅10−55\cdot 10^{-5}, and the gradient norm is clipped at 1. Without these three measures a substantial fraction of initializations diverges to non-finite loss within the first few hundred iterations. Third, the boundary term penalizes both uu and ux​xu_{xx} at the two boundaries, so the loss reads

ℒ=⟨(ℛKS/R0)2⟩+⟨(upred​(x,0)−u⁡(x,0))2⟩+⟨u2+ux​x2⟩∂.\mathcal{L}=\bigl\langle(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{KS}}/R_{0})^{2}\bigr\rangle+\bigl\langle(u_{\mathrm{pred}}(x,0)-u(x,0))^{2}\bigr\rangle+\bigl\langle u^{2}+u_{xx}^{2}\bigr\rangle_{\partial}.

A.2 Kuramoto–Sivashinsky field shift and PINN residual

For completeness, we derive the zero-background form of the generalized Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation used by the PINN. We use the normalization

vt+vx​x+σ​vx​x​x+vx​x​x​x+γ​v​vx+χ​(v2)x​x=0,v_{t}+v_{xx}+\sigma v_{xxx}+v_{xxxx}+\gamma vv_{x}+\chi(v^{2})_{xx}=0, (16)

where γ=2​β\gamma=2\beta, so that the nonlinear convection term integrates to β​v2\beta v^{2} under a traveling-wave reduction. For β=3​σ\beta=3\sigma, substitution of σ=−1\sigma=-1, γ=2​β=6​σ=−6\gamma=2\beta=6\sigma=-6, and χ=3\chi=3 gives

vt+vx​x−vx​x​x+vx​x​x​x−6​v​vx+3​(v2)x​x=0.v_{t}+v_{xx}-v_{xxx}+v_{xxxx}-6vv_{x}+3(v^{2})_{xx}=0. (17)

The exact wave from Kudryashov (2026) is expressed on the background −1/3-1/3. To make the learned field decay to zero away from the pulse, we set

v=u−13,u=v+13.v=u-\frac{1}{3},\qquad u=v+\frac{1}{3}. (18)

Because the shift is constant, all differentiated linear terms are unchanged:

vt=ut,vx=ux,vx​x=ux​x,vx​x​x=ux​x​x,vx​x​x​x=ux​x​x​x.v_{t}=u_{t},\quad v_{x}=u_{x},\quad v_{xx}=u_{xx},\quad v_{xxx}=u_{xxx},\quad v_{xxxx}=u_{xxxx}.

The nonlinear convection term transforms as

−6​v​vx=−6​(u−13)​ux=−6​u​ux+2​ux,-6vv_{x}=-6\left(u-\frac{1}{3}\right)u_{x}=-6uu_{x}+2u_{x}, (19)

whereas the nonlinear diffusion term becomes

v2\displaystyle v^{2} =(u−13)2=u2−23​u+19,\displaystyle=\left(u-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}=u^{2}-\frac{2}{3}u+\frac{1}{9}, (20)
3​(v2)x​x\displaystyle 3(v^{2})_{xx} =3​(u2)x​x−2​ux​x.\displaystyle=3(u^{2})_{xx}-2u_{xx}. (21)

Inserting these expressions into Eq. (17) yields

ut+ux​x−ux​x​x+ux​x​x​x−6​u​ux+2​ux+3​(u2)x​x−2​ux​x=0.u_{t}+u_{xx}-u_{xxx}+u_{xxxx}-6uu_{x}+2u_{x}+3(u^{2})_{xx}-2u_{xx}=0.

Combining the two ux​xu_{xx} terms gives the residual used in the implementation:

ℛKS=ut−ux​x−ux​x​x+ux​x​x​x−6​u​ux+2​ux+3​(u2)x​x.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{KS}}=u_{t}-u_{xx}-u_{xxx}+u_{xxxx}-6uu_{x}+2u_{x}+3(u^{2})_{xx}. (22)
