vex​(x,t)=−13+12​cosh2⁡((x−t−x0)/2),uex​(x,t)=12​cosh2⁡((x−t−x0)/2).v_{\mathrm{ex}}(x,t)=-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2\cosh^{2}((x-t-x_{0})/2)},\qquad u_{\mathrm{ex}}(x,t)=\frac{1}{2\cosh^{2}((x-t-x_{0})/2)}.

Appendix B Baseline SNN model

The Correlation Classwise Network (CCN) Sboev et al. (2025); Kunitsyn et al. (2025) was selected as the baseline model. Its architecture, input encoding, supervisory-signal delivery, and plasticity rule are adopted without modification; the agent’s modifications are restricted to the output-spike-activity decoder. Input expansion using Gaussian receptive fields (GRF) and the bagging ensemble Rybka et al. (2024) are not used because preliminary experiments on MNIST showed no appreciable gain.

The approach is applied to two datasets: MNIST (28×2828\times 28, N=784N=784 spike generators) and the scikit-learn digits Pedregosa et al. (2011) (8×88\times 8, N=64N=64). Both have ten classes, pixel values are normalized by the L1L_{1} norm of the input vector, and the number of output LIF neurons is K=10K=10. The network has two layers: the input layer contains NN spike generators, and the output layer contains KK Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons; the connections are fully connected and trainable, with no lateral connections.

The input vector V=(v1,…,vN)V=(v_{1},\dots,v_{N}) is converted into an array of correlated spike sequences {Si}\{S_{i}\}: a reference sequence S0S_{0} of length NtN_{t} is constructed with constant spacing NrefN_{\mathrm{ref}}; component viv_{i} is interpreted as the target Pearson correlation coefficient between SiS_{i} and S0S_{0}, and SiS_{i} is obtained by randomly removing some spikes from S0S_{0}. Supervision is implemented using two currents applied to the output LIF neurons: for a sample of class kk, a positive current Iexc=107I_{\mathrm{exc}}=10^{7} pA, synchronized with the S0S_{0} spikes with a shift τs\tau_{s}, is applied to the corresponding neuron; the other neurons receive an inhibitory current Iinh=−103I_{\mathrm{inh}}=-10^{3} pA. The weights are adjusted using a local multiplicative STDP rule with a bounding symmetric nearest-neighbor scheme:

Δ​w​(Δ​t)={A+⋅wμ+⋅e−Δt/τ+,Δ​t>0,A−⋅wμ−⋅eΔ​t/τ−,Δ​t<0,\Delta w(\Delta t)=\begin{cases}A^{+}\cdot w^{\mu_{+}}\cdot e^{-\Delta t/\tau_{+}},&\Delta t>0,\\ A^{-}\cdot w^{\mu_{-}}\cdot e^{\Delta t/\tau_{-}},&\Delta t<0,\end{cases}

where Δ​t=tpost−tpre\Delta t=t_{\text{post}}-t_{\text{pre}}, ww is the current weight, A±A^{\pm} are the potentiation and depression amplitudes, τ±\tau_{\pm} are the window time constants, and μ±\mu_{\pm} are the exponents of the weight dependence. The values of all network and STDP-rule parameters are provided in Table 10.

B.1 SNN experimental protocol

MNIST data split.

The standard MNIST test set, containing 10 000 samples, was not used during the agent search. The original training set of 60 000 samples was stratified into training and validation subsets at a 80:20 ratio. The parameters of each proposed decoder were estimated on the training subset, whereas the classification accuracy passed to the agent-search log was calculated only on the validation subset.

After the specified search budget was exhausted, the decoder with the highest validation accuracy was selected. The selected decoder was retrained on the complete original MNIST training set and evaluated once on the standard test set. Test samples, their spike representations, and their labels were not provided to the agents and were not used to select the decoder structure or tune its hyperparameters. The same stratified split of the training set was used in all compared configurations.

digits data split.

Before the agent search began, the digits dataset, containing 1797 samples, was stratified into a development set of 1437 samples and a held-out test set of 360 samples. The test set was not used to calculate metrics passed to the agents, select the decoder structure, or tune its hyperparameters.

Stratified five-fold cross-validation was performed on the development set. The five-fold split was fixed once before the experiments and remained unchanged for all decoders, runs, analyst models, prompt variants, and baseline methods. At each iteration, the proposed decoder was trained five times on four folds and evaluated on the remaining fold. The mean classification accuracy was recorded in the experiment log:

CVAcc⁡(d)=15​∑k=15Acc⁡(d(−k),𝒟(k)),\operatorname{CVAcc}(d)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{k=1}^{5}\operatorname{Acc}\left(d^{(-k)},\mathcal{D}^{(k)}\right), (23)

where d(−k)d^{(-k)} denotes the decoder trained on four folds, and 𝒟(k)\mathcal{D}^{(k)} is the fifth fold excluded from training. The analyst used CVAcc⁡(d)\operatorname{CVAcc}(d) when formulating the next hypothesis.

After the specified search budget was exhausted, the decoder with the highest CVAcc⁡(d)\operatorname{CVAcc}(d) was selected. It was then retrained on all 1437 samples in the development set and evaluated once on the 360 samples in the held-out test set. The resulting test accuracy was not recorded in the agent-search log.

Appendix C Analysis of the best PINN hypotheses

The single-soliton comparison includes Perplexity Sonar (sonar-pro), Claude Opus 4.6, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (Table 5). The agent controls the input transformation FIF_{I} and output transformation FOF_{O}, while the MLP, activation function, collocation points, loss functional, and training schedule remain fixed. The best overall result was obtained by the Claude Opus 4.6 configuration PCDS-LCC-EXP-NLOG-MIXCROSS, which gives Relh=2.21⋅10−5\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=2.21\cdot 10^{-5}, a 24912491-fold reduction from its identity baseline of 5.51⋅10−25.51\cdot 10^{-2}. It uses seven analytical features, including normalized and logarithmic envelopes and two amplitude–time cross-features, while FOF_{O} applies time-gated exponential amplitude and additive phase corrections with separate envelope weights.

The best sonar-pro configuration, tw_nonlinear_pinn_core, gives Relh=1.97⋅10−4\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=1.97\cdot 10^{-4}, a 238238-fold reduction from its identity baseline of 4.69⋅10−24.69\cdot 10^{-2}. Its FIF_{I} supplies a normalized traveling-wave coordinate, normalized time, and a local nonlinearity-density feature; FOF_{O} uses the analytical traveling-wave amplitude and phase and interprets the MLP outputs as bounded amplitude and phase corrections. The best Qwen configuration, LogPhaseHybridNorm, gives Relh=8.86⋅10−3\mathrm{Rel}_{h}=8.86\cdot 10^{-3}, a 5.485.48-fold reduction from its identity baseline of 4.85⋅10−24.85\cdot 10^{-2}. It normalizes the analytical soliton coordinate at the input and reconstructs the field from the analytical amplitude and carrier phase multiplied by learned complex corrections.

All three best configurations exploit the available analytical solution. Their performance should therefore be interpreted as evidence that the framework can discover a useful physics-informed representation, rather than as evidence of performance on problems without a known solution.

Appendix D Repeated PINN runs and statistical analysis

To assess whether the observed improvements are robust to random initialization, we repeated the training procedure for the GNLSE problem with a Gaussian perturbation. We compared the baseline model with two agent-designed configurations: one selected for its low equation residual and the other for its accurate preservation of the physical invariant. Each configuration was successfully trained ten times. Because the random initializations were not matched across configurations, the resulting samples were treated as independent rather than paired. Table 11 summarizes the results.

Both agent-designed configurations reduce the invariant error by more than two orders of magnitude on average relative to the baseline. The residual-selected configuration has a slightly lower mean error and coefficient of variation, although the two distributions overlap substantially. In the original search, the invariant-selected configuration achieved an error of 6.61⋅10−46.61\cdot 10^{-4}, lower than in any of its ten subsequent retrainings. By contrast, the original error of the residual-selected configuration, 1.40⋅10−31.40\cdot 10^{-3}, is close to its repeated-run mean. This contrast indicates a selection effect: the best result found during a search can be more favorable than the performance typically obtained when the same configuration is retrained.

Appendix E Additional classification results

Method-class coverage map.

The aggregate coverage map of decoder method classes from the complete 250-iteration log for the ⟨\langlePerplexity Sonar, detailed prompt⟩\rangle configuration on MNIST is presented in Table 12. Each valid decoder is assigned to one principal class according to the substance of its decision rule, while decoders that explicitly aggregate several predictions are grouped in the “Ensembles” row. The map shows that the analyst spent most of the budget on hybrid ensemble schemes and discriminant analysis, whereas the correlation, margin-based, and argmax classes remained uncovered in this run.

Best decoders and coverage-map ablation.

In the best configuration (Claude Opus 4.6, detailed prompt), the 92.83 % result was obtained by a hybrid method: class-averaged representations serve as centroids, and the decision is based on Mahalanobis distance with class-specific covariance. The pattern is the same for Perplexity Sonar with the detailed prompt: the best decoders belong to LDA/QDA and prototype method classes. These classes use the entire output spike-rate vector, whereas the baseline argmax uses only one of its components. The ablation confirms the role of the coverage map: when it is removed (while the catalog of method classes and Chain-of-Thought are retained), Perplexity Sonar does not reach 90 % during a run, and the best accuracy falls from 92.70 % to 83.18 %; the analyst converges on a narrow set of similar ensemble variations.

The results for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 are provided in Tables 13 and 14, those for Perplexity Sonar in Tables 15 and 16, and those for Claude Opus 4.6 in Tables 17 and 18.

When the simple and detailed prompts were compared, the mean maximum accuracy for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 increased from 79.88±0.00%79.88\pm 0.00\,\% to 85.88±2.42%85.88\pm 2.42\,\%. A positive difference was also observed in all ten pairs and averaged 6.006.00 percentage points. For Claude Opus 4.6, the mean maximum increased from 91.13±0.44%91.13\pm 0.44\,\% to 92.15±0.62%92.15\pm 0.62\,\%. The mean paired difference was 1.021.02 percentage points: a positive effect was observed in 8 of 10 pairs, whereas accuracy decreased by 0.070.07 and 0.110.11 percentage points in two pairs. For Perplexity Sonar, switching to the detailed prompt increased the mean maximum accuracy from 79.88±0.00%79.88\pm 0.00\,\% to 91.76±0.56%91.76\pm 0.56\,\%. A positive difference was observed in all ten pairs, with a mean of 11.8911.89 percentage points.

The coverage-map ablation showed an additional effect of this component of the detailed prompt. For Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, mean accuracy increased from 80.18±0.45%80.18\pm 0.45\,\% to 85.88±2.42%85.88\pm 2.42\,\%, i.e., by 5.705.70 percentage points. In each of the three ablation comparisons, a positive difference was observed in all ten pairs. For Perplexity Sonar, the corresponding values were 82.34±0.70%82.34\pm 0.70\,\% without the map and 91.76±0.56%91.76\pm 0.56\,\% with the map, with a mean increase of 9.429.42 percentage points. For Claude Opus 4.6, the presence of the map increased the mean maximum accuracy from 91.02±0.25%91.02\pm 0.25\,\% to 92.15±0.62%92.15\pm 0.62\,\%; the mean paired increase was 1.141.14 percentage points.

For each model, the statistical significance of differences between the two configurations was assessed using a two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired samples. The null hypothesis stated that neither compared configuration had a systematic advantage: the paired accuracy differences were centered at zero. The alternative hypothesis assumed a systematic difference between the configurations. The test was applied under the assumption of a symmetric distribution of paired differences. For the two-sided test, the WW statistic was defined as the smaller of the rank sums for positive and negative nonzero differences. The significance level was set to α=0.05\alpha=0.05.

For the comparison of the simple and detailed prompts for Claude Opus 4.6, W=5W=5 and p=0.0195p=0.0195 were obtained. For Perplexity Sonar and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, all ten paired differences were positive. Therefore, in both cases the two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test gave the same result: W=0W=0, p=0.001953p=0.001953. The null hypothesis was rejected for all three models at the α=0.05\alpha=0.05 significance level.

Two research questions were tested for the three models: the effect of switching from the simple to the detailed prompt and the effect of including the coverage map in the detailed prompt. Thus, six statistical comparisons were performed, and their results were used to formulate the overall conclusion about the effectiveness of prompt structure.

Testing each hypothesis separately at a significance level of α=0.05\alpha=0.05 does not preserve this level for the full set of comparisons. Specifically, if the six tests were independent and all six null hypotheses were true, the probability of at least one false-positive result would be

1−(1−α)6=1−0.956=0.2649,1-(1-\alpha)^{6}=1-0.95^{6}=0.2649,

i.e., approximately 26.49%26.49\,\%.

To ensure control of the family-wise probability of at least one type I error at 0.050.05, the Holm–Bonferroni correction was applied. This procedure controls the family-wise error even when the statistical tests are dependent. The original pp values were ordered in ascending order and sequentially compared with the thresholds

α6,α5,…,α.\frac{\alpha}{6},\;\frac{\alpha}{5},\;\ldots,\;\alpha.

For the five comparisons with an original p=0.001953p=0.001953, the adjusted value was pHolm=0.0117p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0117. For the comparison of the simple and detailed prompts for Claude Opus 4.6, with an original p=0.0195p=0.0195, pHolm=0.0195p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0195 was obtained. All six adjusted pp values were below 0.050.05, so the corresponding null hypotheses were also rejected after correction for multiple comparisons.

When the detailed prompt with and without the coverage map was compared, all ten paired differences were positive for each of the three models. The same values, W=0W=0, p=0.001953p=0.001953. After applying the Holm–Bonferroni correction across all six comparisons, the adjusted value was pHolm=0.0117p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0117. Consequently, removing the coverage map led to a statistically significant decrease in the maximum accuracy achieved for each model.

After correction for multiple comparisons, the results of all six paired tests remained statistically significant. When switching from the simple to the detailed prompt, the mean accuracy increase was 1.021.02 percentage points for Claude Opus 4.6, 11.8911.89 percentage points for Perplexity Sonar, and 6.006.00 percentage points for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. For Claude Opus 4.6, the two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test gave W=5W=5, an original p=0.0195p=0.0195, and pHolm=0.0195p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0195. For Perplexity Sonar and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, positive differences were obtained in all ten pairs; for each model, W=0W=0, the original p=0.001953p=0.001953, and pHolm=0.0117p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.0117.

Results on the digits dataset.

The same framework was applied to digits 8×88\times 8; the run design was the same as for MNIST. The baseline argmax decoder gives an accuracy of 90.83 %, whereas the best ⟨\langleClaude Opus 4.6, detailed prompt⟩\rangle configuration increases it to 96.67 % (Table 19). The best decoder uses a nonparametric generative classifier based on KDE with a Gaussian kernel in a PCA subspace, and the label is determined using the Bayes rule c^=arg⁡maxc​[log⁡p⁡(f∣c)+log⁡p⁡(c)]\hat{c}=\arg\max_{c}[\log p(f\mid c)+\log p(c)]; hyperparameters were selected using 5-fold cross-validation.

E.1 Decoder search dynamics

In addition to the final accuracy values reported in Tables 2 and 19, the search trajectory itself is of interest: how quickly the agent system finds a decoder that outperforms the baseline and reaches a plateau. Figure 6 shows the maximum accuracy among all decoders proposed up to the current iteration (the cumulative maximum) for each run of the agent system. The MNIST trajectories are collected in Fig. 6, and those for the digits dataset in Fig. 7.

The curves demonstrate a pronounced dependence of convergence speed on the analyst model: with Claude Opus 4.6, the system reaches a plateau by iterations 5–10 (Fig. 6, Claude Opus 4.6 panels), whereas Perplexity Sonar in detailed-prompt mode exhibits stepwise dynamics with accuracy gains at iterations 50, 120, and 170; the system periodically returns to revising hypotheses after long plateaus.

For the simple prompt in the Perplexity Sonar and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 configurations (MNIST), the cumulative maximum does not rise above the baseline level over the entire range of 250 iterations: in these runs, the analyst proposed no decoder that outperformed argmax over aggregated spikes. This contrasts with the detailed-prompt version of the same models, where accuracy begins to increase in the first iterations, indicating the sensitivity of the agent system to the level of detail in the instruction provided to the analyst.

The largest final gain over the baseline was obtained in the detailed-prompt configuration with Claude Opus 4.6 on digits (best-run accuracy 0.96540.9654 versus the digits baseline 0.90850.9085; Table 19), with the increase occurring almost entirely during the first 10 iterations, while the system spends the remaining more than 200 iterations confirming the maximum found without further improvement.

E.2 Decoder catalog and TPOT configuration

The same configuration was used in the classic and sequential TPOT modes, which differ in the search strategy but not in the space of admissible solutions, and in the Random Choice sampler described in Section 4.4. The classic mode used a population of 25 and 9 generations, the sequential mode a population of 1 and 249 consecutive generations. The budget of each mode was 250 evaluated candidates per run. Random Choice does not use TPOT as a search strategy: it draws configurations from the same catalog through independent calls to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and issues as many calls as are needed to record 250 evaluated decoders. Per run it made 347 calls on average.

TPOT selected the best pipeline by mean accuracy in five-fold cross-validation on the training set. After the search was completed, the selected pipeline was retrained on the entire training set and evaluated once on the test set. Test data were not involved in selecting the pipeline structure or its hyperparameters.

Mapping between method classes and operators.

The catalog is based on the decoder taxonomy from the analyst’s detailed prompt. Some substantive classes map to the same scikit-learn estimator with different metrics or hyperparameters. Therefore, the number of TPOT operators does not match the number of classes in the taxonomy. For convenience, the mapping between decoder method classes and TPOT operators is provided in Table 20.

Appendix F Multi-Agent Framework Prompts

The original language of all prompts is Russian.

F.1 Analyst prompt (simple)

# Context You are a leading expert in spiking neural networks (SNNs) and in decoding outputs firing rates into class labels for the MNIST task, with over 20 years of practical experience. You are provided with: - Output spike sequences from 10 output neurons for the training and test datasets; - A JSON table containing experiments conducted using various decoding methods. The goal of this research is to develop a new decoding method that achieves an accuracy of 0.9 or higher (90%+) using a vector of firing rates from 10 output neurons. Important feature of the encoding: Input sequences are encoded by randomly selecting spikes without replacement from a given reference spike sequence. Therefore, the temporal structure of individual spike sequences is unstable across runs and should not be used directly. The informative object for decoding is the vector of firing rates of the 10 output neurons. # Your task Develop a method for decoding the firing-rate vector of the output neurons (dimension: 10) that is not included in the provided JSON experiment table, with the goal of achieving an accuracy of 0.9 or higher. **Available data and abilities:** 1. Output spike sequences vector (zeros and ones) for the training dataset - train_spikes. 2. Output spike sequences vector (zeros and ones) for the test dataset - test_spikes. 3. Correct labels for the training dataset - y_train. 4. You may construct new features and new decoding rules based on firing_rates. When developing a method, clearly distinguish between: - the feature-extraction step from the firing rate vector; - the decision rule step based on these features. Examples of acceptable method classes (which may be combined or extended, but are not limited to): - Normalized argmax over firing rates, optionally with neuron-specific weights and biases; - Rules based on the difference between the two highest firing rates (margin-based); - Class calibration using firing rate statistics for each class (e.g., mean firing rates for each neuron and class) and calss-specific score calculations; - Simple threshold-based and piecewise rules (e.g., small if/then/else/ decision trees based on firing rate thresholds and their combinations). **Limitations:** 1. The output spike trains have already been recorded. You cannot modify the network architecture or encoding method to record different sequences. 2. You cannot use backpropagation to train the proposed method. 3. You may fit method parameters only on the training data (train_spikes and y_train). The test data must be used exclusively for evaluation. 4. Your answer must be presented as a developer specification, including: - a clear description of how features are constructed from firing rates (optional); - a description of the decision rule in analytical form: - formulas for intermediate calculations and for the final transformation from firing rates to a class label; - recommended hyperparameters in the following JSON: `{"decoding_params": {}}`, where `decoding_params` is a dictionary of parameters, such as thresholds, weights, and search ranges. 5. Do not repeat methods that have already been tested and included in the JSON experiment table. 6. If a parameter is best tuned using the training data (e.g., thresholds, weights, or ranges), mark it with the value `"to_fit"` in `decoding_params` and provide a grid of candidate values for iteration. # Experiment Table (JSON):

F.2 Analyst prompt (detailed)

You are a leading neuroinformatics expert (20+ years of experience in spiking neural networks (SNNs) and in decoding outputs firing rates into class labels. Your specialty is developing decoding methods that operate WITHOUT backpropagation, relying exclusively on the statistical properties of output-neuron firing rates. # Dataset: {dataset_name} - Task: {task_description} - Output neurons: (n_neurons) - Classes: {n_classes} - Class labels: {class_labels} - **Target accuracy: {target_accuracy}+** ## Input data - `train_spikes` - a NumPy array `(N_train, {n_neurons})`: the firing rates of the output neurons for the training set; - `test_spikes` - a NumPy array `(N_test, {n_neurons}0`: the firing rates of the output neurons for the test set; - `y_train` - a NumPy array `(N_train,)`: true class labels. ## Encoding Feature Input sequences are generated by randomly sampling spikes from a refrence sequence. Their temporal structure is **unstable** across runs. **Only** the firing rate vector of the {n_neurons} output neurons is informative. # Current experiments on the {dataset_name} Dataset A total of {n_experiments} experiments were conducted. Below is the table (JSON): ```json {current_results_json} ``` # Method Class Coverage Below is an automated analysis of which **method classes** have already been tested and which remain unexplored. Your task is to **prioritize methods from unexplored or underexplored classes** whenever they are theoretically applicable to the given problem. {method_class_coverage_section} **Method class selection rule:** If the table above contains method classes with the status "NOT STUDIED" or "LIMITED DATA", propose a method from one of those classes. Consider an already well-studied class only if you can justify why the proposed variation is fundamntally different from all previously tested methods. # Task Develop a **new** method for decoding firing rate vectors of dimension {n_neurons} that is **not included** in the experiment table, with the goal of achieving an accuracy of **{target_accuracy}+**. ## Mandatory Analytical Process Complete the Chain-of-Thought reasoning: ### Step 1 - Class Coverage Analysis Review the method class coverage table above. - Which classes have not been studied or remain underexplored? - Do any of those classes include methods that are theoretically suitable for this task? - What is the highest accuracy achieved by the methods already tested? - Which properties such as normalization, distance metrics, or regulatization may have contributed to thier performance? ### Step 2 - Failure Analysis Which methods degraded to near-chance accuracy (`~{random_accuracy:.2f}`)? Formulate hypotheses about the possible causes: - overfitting; - matrix degeneracy; - scale instability; - bugs involving array dimensions. **Important:** the failure of a specific implementation does not imply that the entire method class has failed. If kNN or Mahalanobis methods were implemented incorrectly - for example, using a singular matrix or improper normalization - this is a reason to propose **corrected** version rather than abandon the class. ### Step 3 - Selecting a class and synthesizing a method 1. **Priority:** Choose a method from the class with the smallest coverage. 2. If you chose a method from a well-studied class, explain how it fundamentally differs from all previous methofs in that class. 3. Use best practices from successful experiments, such as normalization and regularization, but apply them to a **new type of decision rule**. When developing the method, distinguish between: - **Feature extraction:** constructing features from firing rates. - **Decision rule:** assinging a class label based on these features. ### Step 4 - Self-Check (Required) Before submitting your final answer, verify the following: - [ ] Is the proposed method different from all methods already tested? - [ ] Does the method belong to a **different class** from the one used in most previous experiment? If not, explain why this particular class was selected. - [ ] When working with covariance matrices: was regulatization added (ridge: `Cov + eps * I`, or `np.linalg.pinv`, or diagonal approximation)? - [ ] Does the method scale to {n_classes} classes? - [ ] Is the output an array of integers from 0 to {n_classes_minus_1}? ## Method class Catalog Below is the complete catalog of permitted method classes. Methods from different classes may be combined. **All** methods are implementable using pure NumPy. ### 1. k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) For each test example, find the k nearest neighbors in train_spikes and assign the class by voting. Metrics: Euclidean, Manhattan, Chebyshev, and inverse-distance-weighted voted (1/d). **Tip:** Apply Z-normalization before classification and select k using leave-one-out validation on the training data. ### 2. Mahalanobis Distance Calculate class centroids and covariance matrices, then assign each example to the class with the minimum Mahalanobis distance. Implementable in Numpy via `np.linalg.inv` (or `np.linalg.pinv` for robustness). **Tip:** Apply ridge regularization `Cov_c + eps * I` with eps ~ 1e-4...1e-1. You may also use a pooled covariance matrix instead of the class-specific one. ### 3. Naive Bayes (Gaussian NB) Estimate \mu_c and \sigma_c for each neuron and class. Calculate the log-likelihood of each class as the sum of log-Gaussian probabilites, then select the class with the highest log-posterior using argmax. **Tip:** Apply variance smoothing: \sigma^2 = max(\sigma^2, \epsilon). ### 4. Discriminant Analysis (LDA / QDA) LDA: general covariance matrix + linear discriminant functions. QDA: class-specific covariances. Fisher LDA: projection onto the axis of maximum interclass variance. All variants can be implemented using NumPy linear algebra. **Tip:** For LDA, solve the generalized eigenvalue problem S_w^-1 @ S_b for example using `np.linalg.eigh`. ### 5. Prototypes / Centroids Calculate a centroid for each class, then assign each example to the class with the minimum Euclidean or cosine distance. Options: L1/L2 normalization, weighted centroids, and median centroids for robustness. ### 6. Correlation Decoding Calculate a class-specific score: Score(x, c) = Pearson(x, template_c) or Score(x, c) = cosine(x, template_c). The class template is the mean or median vector. Assign the class label using Argmax over the class scores. ### 7. KDE / Density Estimation For each class, estimate the density p(x|c) from the training data using the kernel method (Gaussian kernel). Classify each example based on argmax p(x|c) * p(c). **Tip:** Select bandwidth using Silverman’s rule or by maximazing accuracy on the training data. ### 8. Rank-based methods Convert firing rates into ranks, work with the order of neurons. Options: rank-based Z-score, Spearman correlation, margin between ranks. ### 9. Margin-based rules Differences between top-K firing rates. Score = fr[top1] - mean(fr[rest]). Options: normalization, Z-score, temperature scaling. ### 10. Softmax Calibration Softmax with temperature fitted to the training data. Plus: biases by class. Z-normalization can be added before softmax. ### 11. Threshold/Piecewise-Specific Rules Cascade threshold rules (mini-trees), if neuron_k > threshold -> class c. Thresholds are selected on the training data. Options: binary codes, one-versus-rest thresholds. ### 12. Ensembles of heterogeneous methods Combine 2-3 **different** methods from the list above with voting or weighted averaging of scores. Select weights on the training data. # Response format - Technical Assignment (TA) Please formulate your answer **strictly** in the following structure: ## 1. Method name A short, unique name (e.g. "ARMD-v2"). ## 2. Method class Indicate which class from the catalog the method belongs to (for example: "kNN,", "Mahalanobis," "Naive Bayes"). ## 3. Method description One paragraph: what the method does, what mathematical idea it is based on. ## 4. Feature extraction Formulas for constructing features from firing rates: - What intermediate values are calculated? - What normalizations/transformations are applied? ## 5. Decision rule Analytical decision-making formula: - How is the score for each class derived from features? - How is the final label derived from scores? ## 6. Hyperparameters JSON: ```json {{"decoding_params":{{...}}}} ``` - Fixed parameters -- with specific values. - Parameters for training -- with the "to_fit" value and a grid specification. # Strict constraints 1. The spike sequences have already been recorded; you cannot modify the SNN. 2. **Prohibited:** backpropagation, gradient descent. 3. Parameter fiting is permitted **only** on train_spikes and y_train. Test data may be used exclusively for evaluation. 4. Do not repeat the methods from the experiment table. 5. Output: one-dimensional numpy array of integers ({class_labels}), of length N_test.

F.3 Coder prompt

# Task The technical specifications are provided below. Please write Python code for them. Write a class that decodes output spike sequences into class labels for the {dataset_name} clasification problem. Decoding must be based on firing rate vectors - i.e., spike counts aggregated over time - from {n_neurons} output neurons. **The class constructor takes exactly 2 parameters:** 1. train_spikes -- a two-dimensional NumPy array of the output firing rates of neurons in the training set of shape (N_train, 10). 2. y_train -- a one-dimensional NumPy array of the class labels of the training set of length (N_train,). **What does the __call__() method accept:** - test_spikes -- a two-dimensional NumPy array of the output firing rates of neurons on the test sample of shape (N_test, 10). **Output of the __call__() method:** y_pred is a one-dimensional Numpy array of length N_test **Restrictions:** - Only standard Python and NumPy are allowed; no other third-party libraries are allowed. - The class name is strictly: Decoding. - The class constructor takes exactly 2 parameters, described above. - If necessary, you can implement a fit method that doesn’t take any arguments and uses only self.train_spikes and self.y_train. - If there are parameters in decoding_params with "to_fit" values, you must implement their tuning on the training data (for example, by selecting thresholds or weights using a grid or another simple method). - After completing the tuning, all hyperparameters (including those marked as "to_fit") should be written to the self.decoding_params attribute as a dictionary with specific values. - The call occurs through the __call__(self, test_spikes) method. - Slice indices must be strictly integer; float/fractional indices are not allowed in slices. - The output is a strictly one-dimensional numpy array of integers from 0 to 9 inclusive, length test_spikes.shape[0]. - By the time the fit method (if implemented) completes, the class must have a self.decoding_params attribute, containing the final values of all the decoding method’s hyperparameters. **Strict withdrawal requirements:** - Return only the decoding code without any comments, text, or additional lines. Blank for this class: ```python class Decoding: def __init__(self, train_spikes, y_train): self.train_spikes = train_spikes self.y_train = y_train def __call__(self, test_spikes): pass # return y_pred ```

F.4 Recorder prompt

Write a short description (approximately one paragraph) of the decoding method and provide the hyperparameters for the decoding method. Compose a short name for the experiment. Provide your answer as JSON with the following structure: ```json { "name": "Short name", "description": "Description of what the Decoding layer does", "decoding_params": {} } ```
